extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, examiners), judges, and law students studying U.S. reissue patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal standards and practical criteria governing when and how a U.S. patent may be surrendered and reissued (including broadened reissues), the statutory limits, procedural requirements, and case-law constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory ground for reissue (invalidation/inoperativeness due to inadvertence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be the subject of a reissue under the statutory law, a patent must be invalid, or at least inoperative, because that fault resulted from a defective or insufficient specification, or from the patentee claiming more than he had a right to claim as new — and that fault must have arisen from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core meritorious ground (derived from Grant v. Raymond and later statutes). The statute's proviso that the fault be inadvertent/accidental/mistaken and non-fraudulent is imperative in all cases. (References: Acts of 1832/1836, section summaries in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Four classes of reissuable faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The remaining faults which make patents reissuable are four in number: (1) invalidity arising from defective description; (2) invalidity arising from insufficient description; (3) invalidity arising from defective claims; (4) inoperativeness arising from insufficient claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories reflect statutory and judicial exposition since 1836. They frame analytical questions when assessing whether a reissue is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'defective' versus 'insufficient' (description/claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Defective' means 'bad' (e.g., obscure in parts though otherwise complete); 'insufficient' means 'lacking' (e.g., clear so far as it goes but omitting parts). A claim may be defective (liable to be misunderstood) or insufficient (clear but too narrow to cover the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishing these meanings matters because the statute uses both words; they are not synonymous and point to different remedial approaches via reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter rule for reissues
rubrics_metrics.description: "No new matter shall be introduced into the specification, nor in case of a machine patent shall the model or drawings be amended, except by leave; but where there is neither model nor drawing, amendments may be made upon proof, satisfactory to the Commissioner, that such new matter or amendment was a part of the original invention, and was omitted from the specification by inadvertence, accident, or mistake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue must not add subject-matter not present in the original; any purported 'new matter' must be shown (to the Commissioner's satisfaction) to have been part of the original invention and omitted by inadvertence. This is a strict constraint on amendments/drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissues that do not add or broaden claims are safe and may be sought at any time
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity or insufficiency arising from defective/insufficient description or defective claims, where that invalidity arose by inadvertence and without fraud, may be remedied by a reissue where the reissue does not add nor broaden any claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such corrective reissues have not been held void in adjudicated cases; they improve public information and can be invoked at any time during the patent's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are the operative parts; inoperativeness from omitted claimed inventions justifies reissue (broadened reissues)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the descriptive part describes multiple allied inventions but the claims cover only one, the patent is operative as to the claimed invention but inoperative as to the others — that inoperativeness suffices to found a right to reissue. Reissues granted to cover such omitted aspects are called 'broadened reissues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not called out by name in early statutes, broadened reissues are authorized by general statutory terms and upheld by the Supreme Court in many cases. They allow claiming matter described but not claimed originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy by disclaimer vs. remedy by reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee has claimed more than he had a right to claim, that fault has generally been curable by disclaimers since 1837; where the matter cannot be excised by disclaimer because it is blended with other matter, rewriting the specification and obtaining a narrower reissue may be the proper remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, disclaimer is preferable because reissue involves loss of rights of action for infringements committed prior to reissue. Use reissue only when disclaimer cannot practically remove the offending subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of inadvertence: acceptable origins vs. forbidden manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadvertence/accident/mistake may be on the part of the patentee or the Patent Office. Examples of acceptable origins include mistake about the state of the art, inadvertent failure to make claims as extensive as invention, or erroneous decisions by the Commissioner (including in interferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unacceptable situations: attempting to reclaim a previously canceled/rejected claim by reissue; making a new claim that, though narrower than a rejected claim, is broader in the same direction than the patent's claim; intentionally omitted claims; using reissue to narrow a disclaimer; or claiming only a machine's function previously done by hand. These scenarios do not satisfy the statutory inadvertence requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and the doctrine barring broadened reissues (Miller v. Brass and time limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to obtain a broadened reissue is lost by a lapse of some time between the date of the original patent and the application for the broadened reissue (Miller v. Brass). The Miller doctrine generally starts the fatal lapse running from the date of the original patent, not from the date the fault was discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have applied the rule liberally: general rule is that delay of two years or more invalidates a broadened reissue unless special circumstances excuse the delay. Shorter delays (even months) have been fatal in plain cases; conversely, complicated specifications or special circumstances (illness, insanity of inventor) may justify longer indulgence. Intervening rights are not required to trigger the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision: scope of reviewability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Commissioner grants a reissue, the question arises whether that decision that statutory grounds exist is conclusive. Findings of the Commissioner based on disputed questions of fact are not reviewable; but where the decision depends on legal interpretation or the effect of undisputed documents or other undisputed evidence, they are reviewable in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically courts debated this; later practice and Supreme Court doctrinal developments have made the practical importance of the issue smaller, but legal review remains possible on legal questions or matters apparent from the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reissue on remedies and term
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue patent is granted to the same inventor, for the same invention, and for the residue of the term of the original patent; the reissued patent is liable to the same defenses as the original and has the same legal effect for causes subsequently accruing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importantly, obtaining a reissue involves the loss of rights of action for infringements committed before the reissue is granted — a key practical disadvantage compared to disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/formal rules: surrender, who may apply, and effect on statutory bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender of the original patent when applying for reissue need not be in writing (parol surrender suffices). The right to receive a reissue extends to executors, administrators, and assigns; where a reissue is to an assignee, the specification must be sworn to by the inventor if he be living. For public-use/on-sale statutory bars, the reissue application is considered appended to the original application, so the two-year bar (public use/on sale) is measured from the original filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural features affect evidentiary issues (presumption of proper surrender) and timing regarding prior public use or sale. Courts accept parol surrender where appropriate; a purported but ineffectual written surrender does not necessarily negate a parol surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances where Commissioner acted beyond statutory grounds (and consequent judicial scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized that the Commissioner of Patents sometimes reissued patents when statutory grounds were arguably absent — e.g., where surrendered patents were neither invalid nor inoperative or the invalidity did not result from inadvertence. It has been an unsettled question historically whether the Commissioner's finding of statutory ground is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: parties should be prepared to litigate the validity of the reissue on legal grounds apparent from the record; review may be limited for factual disputes but available for legal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple reissues and Commissioner discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes and subsequent acts recognized the right of a patentee to demand several reissued patents for distinct parts of the subject-matter of the surrendered patent, and later statutes allowed the Commissioner, in his discretion, to issue several such patents on the applicant's demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits partitioning of a surrendered patent's subject-matter into multiple reissued patents where appropriate; formal requirements (sworn specification, etc.) still apply.
